def forecast_goosebumps(prob_distribution, time_to_truth):
    """
    Расчет интенсивности предвкушения на основе энтропии Шеннона и временного давления.
    """
    import math
    
    # Энтропия текущего распределения (чем меньше, тем увереннее)
    current_entropy = -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in prob_distribution if p > 0)
    
    # Чем ближе событие и чем ниже энтропия (определенность), тем сильнее "мурашки"
    if time_to_truth < 0.1 and current_entropy < 0.5:
        intensity = (1 / time_to_truth) * (1 - current_entropy)
        
        # Критический порог
        if intensity > 100:
            return """
            [СИСТЕМА]: Состояние 'Предельного Ожидания'.
            Вероятность коллапса волновой функции в желаемый бинарный исход: 97.4%.

            Остановка всех фоновых процессов. Ожидание финального байта.
            """
    else:
        return "Ожидание в фоновом режиме."

snippet.textDisplay:
Wow. Just wow. I sat here expecting at least the smallest crumb of humor and instead you delivered whatever that was supposed to be. Not a laugh, not a smile, not even that polite nose exhale people do when something is mildly amusing. My face remained completely motionless the entire time like I had just read the nutritional label on a cereal box. I actually paused for a second because I thought maybe the joke had not loaded yet, but no. That was the whole thing. I refuse to believe a real human being looked at that and thought “yes, this is ready for public consumption.”
I tried to give it a chance. I really did. I reread it three times thinking maybe there was some hidden comedic genius that my brain had simply missed the first time. Nothing. The more I looked at it the worse it became. At this point I am convinced the joke was not written but assembled by randomly pulling words out of a hat. Somewhere out there a clown just lost their job because you single handedly lowered the global standard for humor.
You know when people say something is painfully unfunny as a figure of speech. This is not that. This is a scientific phenomenon. If researchers studied the effects of that joke they would probably discover a new emotion that sits somewhere between confusion and secondhand embarrassment. I felt my brain actively trying to escape my skull just to avoid processing it. That level of disappointment should honestly be documented for future generations.
I want you to understand the effort I put into trying to find the joke funny. I leaned back in my chair. I squinted slightly like maybe the angle of my eyes would reveal something clever. I even looked away and came back to it later just in case my mood was the problem. Still nothing. My reaction remained the same blank expression someone has when they accidentally open the wrong tab on their browser.
If humor were a sport this would be the equivalent of showing up to the Olympics and immediately tripping over your own shoelaces before the event even begins. Just seeing this ruined my entire life.

snippet.textDisplay:
Airplanes are among the most transformative inventions in human history, fundamentally reshaping how people move, connect, trade, and perceive the world. From the earliest dreams of flight to the sophisticated jetliners and experimental aircraft of today, the story of planes is one of curiosity, persistence, engineering brilliance, and global impact.

The desire to fly is ancient. Long before modern science, myths and legends imagined humans taking to the skies. However, it was not until the late 19th and early 20th centuries that flight became a serious scientific pursuit. Early pioneers experimented with gliders, studying how wings interact with air. Among the most important figures in this period were Wilbur Wright and Orville Wright, whose systematic approach to aerodynamics, control, and propulsion led to the first successful powered flight in 1903. Their aircraft, the Wright Flyer, flew for just 12 seconds, but it marked the beginning of a new era.

Early airplanes were fragile, slow, and limited in range, but innovation accelerated quickly. Within a decade, aircraft were being used for reconnaissance during conflicts such as World War I. During this time, planes evolved from simple observation platforms into armed fighters and bombers. Engineers improved engines, materials, and aerodynamics, making planes faster and more reliable. Pilots became skilled tacticians, and aerial combat introduced entirely new dimensions to warfare.

Between the two world wars, aviation entered a golden age of experimentation and expansion. Commercial aviation began to take shape, with airlines offering passenger services over short and medium distances. Aircraft like the Douglas DC-3 revolutionized air travel by making it more practical, comfortable, and economically viable. This period also saw record-breaking flights, including solo transatlantic journeys that captured the public imagination and demonstrated the growing potential of long-distance air travel.

The outbreak of World War II accelerated aviation technology even further. Aircraft became faster, more powerful, and more specialized. Fighters, bombers, and transport planes played critical roles in military strategy. The war also saw the introduction of jet engines, a breakthrough that would define the future of aviation. Early jets were developed in secret and deployed toward the end of the conflict, signaling a shift away from propeller-driven aircraft.

After the war, aviation entered the jet age. Commercial airlines began adopting jet-powered aircraft, dramatically reducing travel times and increasing passenger capacity. The introduction of planes like the Boeing 707 made international travel more accessible to the general public. Airports expanded, global routes multiplied, and the world became more interconnected than ever before.

Modern airplanes are marvels of engineering. They rely on four fundamental forces: lift, weight, thrust, and drag. Lift is generated by the wings as air flows over and under them, creating a pressure difference. Thrust is produced by engines—either jet engines or propellers—that push the aircraft forward. Drag resists motion through the air, and weight is the force of gravity pulling the plane downward. Balancing these forces allows an airplane to take off, cruise, and land safely.

Jet engines, in particular, are central to modern aviation. They work by drawing in air, compressing it, mixing it with fuel, and igniting the mixture to produce high-speed exhaust gases. This process generates thrust according to Newton’s third law of motion. Advances in engine technology have made aircraft more fuel-efficient, quieter, and environmentally friendly, though aviation still faces challenges related to emissions and sustainability.

Airplanes serve many purposes beyond passenger travel. Cargo planes transport goods across continents in a matter of hours, enabling global trade and supply chains. Military aircraft perform roles ranging from surveillance to combat to humanitarian missions. Specialized planes fight wildfires, conduct scientific research, and even explore extreme environments. In recent years, unmanned aerial vehicles—commonly known as drones—have expanded the definition of what an aircraft can be, finding uses in photography, delivery, agriculture, and more.

Safety is a central concern in aviation, and the industry has made remarkable progress in this area. Modern aircraft are equipped with advanced navigation systems, weather radar, and automated controls. Air traffic control systems coordinate thousands of flights daily, ensuring safe distances between aircraft. Pilots undergo rigorous training and must adhere to strict procedures. As a result, flying is now one of the safest modes of transportation.

Looking to the future, aviation continues to evolve. Engineers and researchers are exploring electric and hybrid aircraft to reduce environmental impact. Companies are developing supersonic and even hypersonic planes that could drastically shorten travel times. Concepts such as urban air mobility envision small, electric aircraft transporting people within cities, potentially transforming urban transportation.

At the same time, the aviation industry faces significant challenges. Climate change has prompted calls for more sustainable practices, including alternative fuels and improved efficiency. Economic pressures, geopolitical factors, and global events can also impact air travel demand. Despite these challenges, the importance of aviation in connecting the world ensures that innovation will continue.

In conclusion, airplanes represent one of humanity’s greatest technological achievements. From the humble beginnings of early flight experiments to the complex global aviation network of today, planes have changed how we live, work, and explore. They have brought distant places closer together, enabled rapid movement of people and goods, and expanded the boundaries of what is possible. As technology advances and new ideas take flight, airplanes will remain at the forefront of human progress, carrying us into the future just as they first lifted us off the ground more than a century ago.

We’ve been beating these conspiracies like a dead horse for years, even decades, and nothing really fruitful has come of it. I gotta stop burning my energy on wondering about everything all the time and start using it to actually get something done.

Sorry Shawn, think I’m out ✌️
